extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of natural theology / early-modern philosophy interested in the possibility of bodily resurrection and personal identity
extracted.subtask_description: A systematic defence (early-modern theological/philosophical) of the possibility that persons will be raised with their own bodies, giving conceptual criteria for what counts as the 'same' or 'own' body and answering naturalistic objections (cannibalism, emaciation, loss/accretion of matter, Scripture texts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Possibility test: absence of contradiction
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove the possibility of resurrection one need only show that it involves no contradiction or impossibility; it is not necessary to exhibit a full mechanical demonstration of how it occurs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The defender must show a way (or at least that one can imagine a way) the event could occur without logical contradiction. Natural ignorance of the mechanism does not amount to impossibility; divine power can supply what natural explanation lacks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between 'own' body and visible body
rubrics_metrics.description: There is an essential difference between a person's 'own' (proper) body and the visible, tangible body: the visible body can have parts joined, separated, replaced and altered, while the 'own' body remains fixed as the same person's proper body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use linguistic examples (we say someone is '80 years old' of their own body, but 'weighs 200' of the visible body) and thought experiments about accretion/separation of parts to show the conceptual distinction; this supports identity despite bodily change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Samen/seed principle as criterion of identity
rubrics_metrics.description: A subtle, simple principle (called the 'Samen' or seed) that underlies the visible body can be the proper or own body for purposes of resurrection; if this Samen remains and is unfolded/clothed by matter, identity is preserved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogies: a grain sown becomes a different-looking plant yet is 'the same' seed's result; the Samen may be expanded and clothed with either the same matter or other matter God pleases to use at resurrection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity despite loss or accretion of matter
rubrics_metrics.description: A person remains the same although during life vast quantities of material that once composed their visible body are lost and replaced; loss or addition of matter over time does not destroy the identity of the own body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical calculation (e.g. an 80-year life with daily intake) and examples of ordinary nourishment show most original particles have been replaced, yet we still call the person the same; therefore replacement or mixture of particles at resurrection does not preclude identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential role of solid structures (nerves/membranes) vs. transient fluids
rubrics_metrics.description: The propre/own body is principally constituted by solid structures (nerves, membranes, tubes, bones) rather than by transient fluids (blood, chyle, milk), which are continually changed and may cease at death without destroying identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Since fluids are frequently exchanged and lost, identity is located in the more persistent structural parts; this supports re-identification even when visible fluids differ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emaciation or wasting does not break identity
rubrics_metrics.description: Extreme emaciation (as in severe sickness) leaves an individual still the same person; the visible body's diminished bulk does not change the identity of the own body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use clinical anecdotes of people reduced to skeleton-like condition and later restored to flesh to show that a much-altered visible body is nevertheless the same person's body.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identity does not require identical material composition
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not necessary that the resurrected body be made of the very same matter as the pre-death visible body; God may fill the Samen with other matter and still produce the same person's body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare recovery from illness (new food becoming part of the body) and the Pauline seed-analogy; the criterion is continuity of the proper principle, not material identity of particles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Samen expansion can yield different life-states (child vs adult)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Samen, if preserved, can be unfolded and filled such that a dead child might be raised as either a child or as a full-grown adult depending on how it is expanded and clothed at resurrection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thought-experiments: if growth had continued, additional matter would have been used to fill out the body; the same Samen is compatible with either outcome, showing flexibility of the identity-criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Response to cannibalism objection: consumption does not prevent reconstitution
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if a cannibal devours many persons, the own bodies of the devoured can still be reconstituted at resurrection because the solid particles (or the Samen) that constitute each proper body can be separated, discharged, or recomposed rather than being irretrievably mixed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical observation (digestion separates nutritious juices from solids) and the natural course of separation of particles support that the devoured bodies' proper parts could be separated and appear whole at resurrection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical/natural observations as supporting evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Daily observations about bodies (loss of material, change of fluids, regeneration after illness) provide evidence that the reconstitution of a person's own body is not impossible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collectors of arguments should marshal empirical cases (bleeding, emaciation and recovery, bodily growth) to show there is no natural contradiction in the idea of reconstitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scriptural analogies do not conflict with physical possibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Scriptural texts (e.g. Paul’s grain/seed comparison) which suggest that the resurrection body need not be numerically identical in material composition are not inconsistent with natural-philosophical accounts of bodily identity; apparent textual objections can be reconciled once one distinguishes kinds of body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret difficult passages in light of the distinction between visible and own bodies and the Samen-analogy; Scripture’s claim that 'God gives it a body as he pleases' supports the conceptual account.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion of explanatory sufficiency rather than full mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: It is sufficient for the defender to indicate a manner in which resurrection may be effected that includes no contradiction; providing a complete natural mechanism is not required, because divine agency may operate beyond natural explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on showing a coherent account (Samen + divine filling, persistence of solid structures) rather than attempting to derive the resurrection from existing physical laws alone.
